section.title: The Oracle against Damascus
section.sectionRationale: This is one panel in the long gallery of oracles against the nations, chapters 13 through 23, in which the LORD of Hosts pronounces sentence on the powers that surround His people. Here Damascus, capital of Aram, falls together with Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, because the two had joined hands in a political alliance rather than trusting the LORD.
section.thesis: Damascus and Ephraim, allied together against Judah, fall together under the LORD's judgment, for both leaned on each other rather than on the Rock of their salvation; yet even from the wreckage a remnant will turn from idols to look at last to their Maker.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the burden against Damascus and Ephraim; the splendor of Jacob fading to a few gleanings; the turn to the Maker on that day; the charge of forgetting the Rock of refuge; and the roar and sudden rout of the nations.

units.label: The burden against Damascus and Ephraim

verses.text: This is the {{massa|burden}} against Damascus: “Behold, Damascus is no longer a city; it has become a heap of ruins.
The cities of Aroer are forsaken; they will be left to the flocks, which will lie down with no one to fear.
The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the sovereignty from Damascus. The remnant of Aram will be like the splendor of the Israelites,” declares the LORD of Hosts.

units.label: The splendor of Jacob fades to a few gleanings

verses.text: “In that day the splendor of Jacob will fade, and the fat of his body will waste away,
as the reaper gathers the standing grain and harvests the ears with his arm, as one gleans heads of grain in the Valley of Rephaim.
Yet gleanings will remain, like an olive tree that has been beaten, two or three berries atop the tree, four or five on its fruitful branches,” declares the LORD, the God of Israel.

units.label: In that day, men will look to their Maker
units.note: the mercy folded into the judgment

verses.text: In that day men will look to their Maker and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel.
They will not look to the altars they have fashioned with their hands or to the Asherahs and incense altars they have made with their fingers.
In that day their strong cities will be like forsaken thickets and summits, abandoned to the Israelites and to utter desolation.
For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and failed to remember the {{tsur|Rock}} of your refuge. Therefore, though you cultivate delightful plots and set out cuttings from exotic vines,
though on the day you plant you make them grow, and on that morning you help your seed sprout, yet the harvest will vanish on the day of disease and incurable pain.

units.label: The roar and sudden rout of the nations
units.note: terror in the evening, gone by morning

verses.text: Alas, the tumult of many peoples; they rage like the roaring seas and clamoring nations; they rumble like the crashing of mighty waters.
The nations rage like the rush of many waters. He rebukes them, and they flee far away, driven before the wind like chaff on the hills, like tumbleweeds before a gale.
In the evening, there is sudden terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us and the lot of those who plunder us.

massa.gloss: A burden, or a load carried, and by extension a weighty pronouncement or oracle. Nearly every oracle against the nations in Isaiah 13 to 23 opens with this word: the prophet is handed a heavy word from the LORD that he must carry to the nations and then deliver.

tsur.gloss: Rock, a common Old Testament title for the LORD as an unshakable refuge and source of salvation. To forget the Rock is to forget the very ground of safety; the New Testament identifies this Rock with Christ, the spiritual Rock that followed Israel, 1 Corinthians 10:4.

basic.context: Isaiah 17 pairs Damascus, capital of Aram, with Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, because the two nations had formed a military alliance against Judah, the very crisis behind Isaiah 7's sign of Immanuel. The chapter announces that both allies will fall together, their glory reduced to a few gleaned olives, yet promises that a remnant will finally turn from idols to their Maker.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical oracle fulfilled substantially when Assyria crushed both Damascus and the northern kingdom in the 730s and 720s BC. It describes God's actual judgment on a doomed political alliance; it is not a timeless formula guaranteeing that every alliance will fail, but it does teach that trusting anyone other than the LORD leaves people exposed.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter opens with massa, a burden, the same weighty word that heads each oracle against the nations. At its center Israel is charged with forgetting the tsur, the Rock, of their salvation, a title later applied to Christ Himself, the spiritual Rock that followed Israel and the sure foundation stone of Isaiah 28:16.
basic.typology: The forgotten Rock of refuge anticipates Christ, the Rock who is never forgotten by the Father and who becomes, in Isaiah 28:16 and 1 Peter 2:6, the tested cornerstone on which believers stand secure. The remnant who turn from idols to their Maker foreshadow all who turn from empty things to worship God through Christ.
basic.christ: Israel forgot the Rock of their salvation and planted foreign vines that yielded no harvest; Christ is the Rock who was never forgotten by the Father and who alone gives a harvest that does not fail. Paul later calls Christ the spiritual Rock that followed Israel in the wilderness, 1 Corinthians 10:4, and Peter calls Him the living stone believers are built upon, 1 Peter 2:4 to 6.
basic.god: God is sovereign over international politics: an alliance formed in defiance of Him unravels under His hand, no matter how strong it looks. Yet even in pronouncing this judgment, He leaves room for mercy, gleanings on the branch and a remnant who look at last to their Maker.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 16:5-9 records the actual Syro-Ephraimite alliance and its collapse. Isaiah 7:1-9 is Isaiah's earlier confrontation with this same crisis. 1 Corinthians 10:4 identifies the Rock with Christ. Isaiah 28:16, echoed in 1 Peter 2:6, names the tested cornerstone laid in Zion.
basic.oneStory: This oracle shows that no alliance apart from the LORD can stand, and that even in judgment God leaves a remnant who turn to their Maker. The forgotten Rock of Israel's refuge is Christ, who was never forgotten by the Father and who alone gathers a harvest of worshipers from every people who turn to Him.

context.literary:
The oracle is built from five short panels that alternate between ruin and remnant. Verses 1 to 3 announce the end of the partnership in the language of a razed city and a removed throne. Verses 4 to 6 turn to Jacob and describe his decline with two harvest pictures, the reaper's arm and the beaten olive tree. Verses 7 and 8 lift the eyes toward a different kind of looking. Verses 9 to 11 return to loss and give the reason, which is forgetfulness. Verses 12 to 14 close with a roar of nations that is silenced in a single night. The phrase 'in that day' marks the joints, in verses 4, 7 and 9, so that the reader sees one day of the LORD from three angles.

The Hebrew word kavod, glory or splendor, links the first two panels. In verse 3 the remnant of Aram is said to be like 'the splendor of the Israelites,' and in verse 4 'the splendor of Jacob will fade.' The irony is bitter: Aram's leftovers will be exactly as glorious as Israel's, which is to say hardly glorious at all. Verbs of looking shape the middle of the chapter. Men will 'look' to their Maker in verse 7 and will not 'look' to their altars in verse 8, and the next oracle opens with a distant land whose envoys scurry about while the LORD 'looks on' quietly, 18:4. The cry that begins verse 12 is the same short word, hoy, as the 'Woe' that begins 18:1, so the last stanza of chapter 17 works as a hinge that ties Damascus to Cush.

Notice also the scale. Kingdoms and fortresses fill verses 1 to 3, a handful of olives fills verse 6, and then whole oceans roar in verses 12 and 13. Isaiah shrinks Israel's pride to berries on a branch and lets the world thunder, only to show that the thunder itself is small before one rebuke from God.
context.historical:
The setting is the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of about 735 to 732 BC. Rezin of Aram, ruling from Damascus, and Pekah son of Remaliah of Israel tried to force the young Judean king Ahaz into an anti-Assyrian coalition, and when he refused they marched on Jerusalem, Isaiah 7:1-2 and 2 Kings 16:5. Isaiah met Ahaz at the end of the aqueduct of the upper pool and told him not to fear 'these two smoldering stubs of firewood,' Isaiah 7:4, adding that Ephraim would be shattered as a people within sixty-five years, 7:8. Ahaz ignored him. He stripped the temple and palace treasuries and sent the silver and gold to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria, who responded by marching on Damascus, capturing it and putting Rezin to death, 2 Kings 16:7-9. Assyria had already taken Galilee and Gilead from Israel, 2 Kings 15:29, and Samaria itself fell after a three year siege, 2 Kings 17:5-6, in about 722 BC.

Aram and Israel had been enemies long before they were allies. Under Hazael, Damascus had ravaged Israel's land east of the Jordan 'from Aroer by the Arnon Valley,' 2 Kings 10:32-33, which may be why verse 2 mentions 'the cities of Aroer.' That Aroer lay on the Arnon, Deuteronomy 2:36. The reference is awkward in the Hebrew text and scholars disagree about it, but the picture is plain: border towns left to the flocks. Amos had announced the fall of Damascus decades earlier, Amos 1:3-5, so Isaiah is adding his voice to a long word, not starting a rumor.

Verse 8 names Asherahs and incense altars, a reminder that eighth century Israel had mixed the worship of the LORD with the cults of the land. Some interpreters think the 'delightful plots' of verses 10 and 11 describe gardens forced into bloom in a day for a fertility rite. That is a proposal, not a certainty, and the verse makes its point either way: neighbours of Judah were gardening for a harvest the LORD had already cancelled.

Judah is listening too. The last stanza speaks of 'those who loot us,' verse 14, and Assyria would indeed pour into Judah, Isaiah 8:7-8, before an overnight deliverance outside Jerusalem in 701 BC, Isaiah 37:36.
context.canonical:
Within Isaiah the chapter answers Isaiah 7 and 8. Isaiah 8:4 had said that before a boy could cry 'Father' or 'Mother' the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria would be carried off by Assyria's king, and in Isaiah 10:9 the Assyrian boasts, 'Is not Samaria like Damascus?' Chapter 17 is God's own commentary on the same events. The beaten olive tree of verse 6 returns in Isaiah 24:13 as a picture of the whole earth, so that Israel's fate becomes a sample of the world's. The gleaning law in Deuteronomy 24:20 had reserved whatever remains on a beaten olive tree for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow, a quiet background to the word remnant. Isaiah 10:20-22 states the doctrine outright: the survivors 'will no longer depend on him who struck them, but they will truly rely on the LORD.'

The charge in verse 10 repeats the charge of Moses' song, where Jeshurun 'scorned the Rock of his salvation' and 'forgot the God who gave you birth,' Deuteronomy 32:15-18. Isaiah is preaching from the old script. The title Rock runs on through Isaiah 26:4, 'GOD the LORD is the Rock eternal,' and into the New Testament, where Paul says the spiritual rock that accompanied Israel 'was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4, and Peter gathers Isaiah 28:16 to say that the one who believes in the cornerstone 'will never be put to shame,' 1 Peter 2:6.

The roaring peoples of verses 12 to 14 belong to a wide biblical habit of picturing hostile nations as a sea that God quiets, Psalm 46:1-3 and Psalm 2:1-4. The verb for God's rebuke, which the BSB gives in verse 13 as 'He rebukes them,' is the one used of the waters at creation: 'At Your rebuke the waters fled,' Psalm 104:7. Isaiah 37:36 then shows the pattern at work when an entire army is gone by morning.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah was not writing to Damascus. These oracles were heard in Jerusalem, and their first aim was to loosen Judah's grip on two opposite temptations. One was fear: the threat of Aram and Ephraim had made Ahaz tremble, and the roar of the nations in verses 12 and 13 would have sounded very like the din Judah heard at its own gates. The other was borrowed confidence: looking to Assyria, or to Egypt later, as a protector. Isaiah tells his hearers that the one thing the great powers have in common is that they are all temporary, and that the only stable thing in the picture is the God who can rebuke a sea.

He also wants Judah to see itself in the mirror held up to Ephraim. Ephraim is charged with forgetting the God of its salvation, and Judah has just done the same thing with its treasury and its treaty. The oracle is therefore a warning dressed as news about a neighbour. The hoped for response is the one verse 7 describes: to lift the eyes from the work of one's own hands to the Holy One of Israel, and to trust Him when the harvest of human plans fails.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what God did and will do to a particular alliance; it does not command anyone to fight, to flee or to avoid treaties as such. Judah's rulers were not condemned for making agreements in general but for making this one in place of the trust Isaiah had just urged on them, Isaiah 7:9. A reader who turns the chapter into a ban on every partnership has missed the point, and a reader who treats it as proof that every strong coalition will collapse has missed it in another way.

What does carry forward is the pattern of looking. Verses 7 and 8 contrast two objects of attention, the Maker and the altars made by fingers, and verse 10 explains how a people drifts from one to the other, by forgetting. The application is therefore to remembering, a discipline the New Testament keeps alive in the Lord's Supper, Luke 22:19, and to the regular practice of examining what we actually run to when trouble comes.

debates.question: Who are the people who 'look to their Maker' in verses 7 and 8?

views.label: A remnant of Ephraim after the Assyrian blow
views.case: The surrounding verses concern Israel's cities and altars, and the people who give up their man made altars are the same ones who had trusted them. On this reading some northern Israelites, humbled by Assyria's conquest, turned back to the LORD. There is some support in the record that individuals from the north did so: under Hezekiah, 'some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem,' 2 Chronicles 30:11.

views.label: Judah and the faithful of Israel in Hezekiah's day
views.case: Others point out that Isaiah's hearers are in Jerusalem and that the chapter is spoken to a Judean audience. Hezekiah's reform removed altars and Asherahs, 2 Kings 18:4, so the verses could be describing the very turning that Isaiah hoped for in his own generation.

views.label: Humanity at the end of the age
views.case: The Hebrew speaks of 'man' in the singular in verse 7, and the phrase 'in that day' elsewhere in Isaiah regularly reaches toward the last days, for example Isaiah 2:2-4 and 25:9. On this view the verse looks to a worldwide turning to the Maker.

debates.bearing: These readings are not mutually exclusive. Isaiah often lets a near turning and a far turning stand in the same verse, and the New Testament's picture of Gentiles and Jews turning together to the same Holy One of Israel fits the widest sense without cancelling the narrower ones. What is not open to debate is the contrast between looking to the Maker and looking to what our hands have made.

debates.question: Are verses 12 to 14 about Assyria in 701 BC, or about the nations in general?

views.label: Assyria's army at the gates of Jerusalem
views.case: The speaker is Judah ('those who loot us'), the language of seas and tumult matches Isaiah 8:7-8, where Assyria is the flood, and Isaiah 37:36 records a night in which Assyria's camp was struck down, giving the 'before morning, they are no more' of verse 14 a striking historical fit.

views.label: All hostile nations and the last assault
views.case: Because the verses speak of 'many peoples' and 'clamoring nations' rather than of one king, and because later prophets use the same imagery for a final gathering of nations against God's city, for instance Psalm 46:1-3 and Psalm 2:1-4, some take it as a typical scene that is not tied to one year.

debates.bearing: The passage is written in a form that fits both. A prophet who has just surveyed several kingdoms is giving the general law of how the LORD deals with nations that rage against His people, and 701 BC is its clearest instance. Either way the comfort is the same, that the roar is loud and the end is quick.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word worth slowing down for is kavod, translated 'splendor' in verses 3 and 4. In its most common use it means weight, the substance and honor that make a person or a nation count for something. The same word is used of Aram's remnant and of Jacob in two consecutive verses, which means the prophet is making a play on weight: the heavy glory of Jacob will waste away, like the 'fat of his body,' and what is left will have no more weight than Aram's. The image fits a body that is wasting, and it is also a sober reversal for a people who thought of themselves as established.

Next is the verb of looking in verses 7 and 8, sha'ah, to turn the gaze toward something and rely on it. It is not the common word for seeing. Isaiah uses it again when he condemns the men who go down to Egypt and 'do not look to the Holy One of Israel,' Isaiah 31:1. A different verb for looking, nabat, appears when the LORD says He will 'look on' quietly in 18:4, and when Isaiah complains in Isaiah 22:11 that his people built a reservoir 'but you did not look to the One who made it.' Verse 7 names the object of true looking as 'their Maker,' the One who made them, and the 'Holy One of Israel,' a title that is characteristic of Isaiah's book. Looking is how the book measures faith.

Third is the vocabulary of strength. The 'fortress' of verse 3 and the 'strong cities' of verse 9 belong to the same word family as the 'refuge' in verse 10, where God is called 'the Rock of your refuge.' The Hebrew thus sets true and false strongholds side by side, and the reader is invited to see that the cities named strong will be abandoned while the One named a refuge stays. 'Rock,' tsur, is itself a great covenant title for God, as in 1 Samuel 2:2, 'there is no Rock like our God.'

Fourth, verse 6 speaks of 'gleanings,' the leftovers of a harvest. The beaten olive tree with 'two or three berries atop the tree' is not a picture of nothing. Gleanings are what the law set aside for those in need, Deuteronomy 24:20, and the same image carries a tone of both scarcity and provision in Isaiah 24:13. The prophet's term for the survivors is not an accident of vocabulary but a theology of what is left in God's hand.

Finally, verse 13 says that God 'rebukes' the nations, a verb that elsewhere describes His command over the sea, Psalm 104:7. The tumbleweed in the same verse is the word translated that way in Psalm 83:13, where the psalmist prays for enemies to be made 'like tumbleweed, O my God, like chaff before the wind.' Verse 11 is among the hardest verses in the chapter to translate, and some versions take the 'harvest' as a heap, so that the sense is a heap of produce that comes to nothing on a day of sickness; the BSB's reading and that one both say that the sown field yields grief.

typology.fulfillment: Israel's failure was to forget the Rock, and the remedy is to look to Him. Paul says the spiritual rock that accompanied the people in the wilderness 'was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. The escalation is that God does not leave a forgetful people with only a title, but lays a real stone in Zion, 'a tested stone, a precious cornerstone,' Isaiah 28:16, and Peter says those who believe in Him 'will never be put to shame,' 1 Peter 2:6. The same stone is also a stumbling stone to those who will not look to Him, Romans 9:32-33 and Luke 20:17-18. The type falls short because a rock in a desert gave water for a season; Christ gives living water that does not run dry, John 4:14.

The few olives left on the highest branches are a picture of how God preserves a people through judgment. The pattern recurs in Elijah's day, when the LORD reserved seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal, and Paul applies it to his own time: 'at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace,' Romans 11:4-5. In Christ the remnant narrows to one faithful Israelite who bears the judgment and then opens the branches to many, so that Gentiles are grafted in, Romans 11:17-24. The type falls short because the survivors in Isaiah's day were spared by God's mercy but not made righteous by it, while those who are in Christ are counted righteous in Him.

Isaiah has the LORD rebuke a roaring ocean of nations so that they flee like chaff. In Mark 4:39 Jesus 'rebuked the wind and the sea,' and the disciples ask 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' The Gospel writer has arranged the scene so that the question is answered by the Psalms and Isaiah: only the LORD silences the seas. The escalation is that the Rebuker steps into the boat. The correspondence is a pattern of divine authority rather than a prediction, and the type falls short in that Isaiah's rebuke ends hostile armies, while Jesus' rebuke also reaches the fear inside His own friends.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most plainly through its title for God, the Rock. Isaiah charges that Israel 'forgot the Rock of your refuge,' and the New Testament tells us who that Rock is. Paul writes that the spiritual rock that accompanied Israel in the wilderness 'was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. Peter then draws the Zion stone of Isaiah 28:16 into the church's confession, 1 Peter 2:4-6, and Jesus applies Psalm 118 to Himself when He tells the leaders of the temple that 'the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,' Luke 20:17. So the God Israel forgot is the very God who comes in the flesh, and the answer to forgetting is not only a command to remember but a Person to look to.

It leads to Christ by contrast. The people in verses 10 and 11 plant, tend and protect, and nothing comes of it. The day arrives when the harvest 'will vanish.' Jesus tells a very different story about a seed: 'unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed; but if it dies, it bears much fruit,' John 12:24. Where human gardening ends in grief, His death and burial produce a harvest that includes every nation, Revelation 5:9.

It leads to Christ by the remnant and by the sea. The remnant that Isaiah sees, a few berries on the branch, is the world as God had seen it from the start, and the gospel shows that remnant gathered round one Man, Romans 11:5. The nations that roar like the sea are silenced by a rebuke, and Mark shows the One who gives that rebuke asleep in a boat on a stormy night, Mark 4:39-41. The disciples' fear and the question they ask is the right one, and Isaiah 17 helps supply its answer.

There is also the line from Isaiah 8, which stands behind this chapter's whole political setting: 'For God is with us,' Isaiah 8:10. Ahaz would not trust it, and the book calls the promised child Immanuel. Chapter 17 is what it looks like for that name to be true of a faithless people's enemies: Damascus and Samaria fall because God is with Judah, in spite of Judah. The same promise finds its fullest form in Jesus, whom Matthew names Immanuel, Matthew 1:23.

We should be careful not to force Christ into every detail. The olive tree in verse 6 and the plots of verse 10 are not codes. The legitimate links are the titles, the pattern of remnant and rebuke, and the invitation in verse 7 to look to the Holy One of Israel, who is Jesus of Nazareth.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows is that God's reach is not confined to Israel's borders. He announces the fate of Damascus, the capital of a neighbouring power, and He calls Himself 'the LORD of Hosts' over the whole scene, verse 3. The nations are not outside His story. Isaiah 14:26-27 had already said that the plan He has devised is 'for the whole earth,' and no one can thwart it, and chapter 17 is that plan applied to one alliance. Kings who believe they are acting on their own initiative find that their joint venture had a date set for its end.

Second, the God of Isaiah 17 is a God of memory. His charge against His people is not an offense of violence but of amnesia: 'you have forgotten the God of your salvation.' That reveals something about Him. He is not an abstract power but the God who saves, who has a history with His people and expects to be remembered as the One who rescued them. Forgetting Him is both ingratitude and a loss of the one reliable fact about the world.

Third, He is just, and He is exact. The language of verses 4 to 6 fits the sin and the sentence together: a nation that thought of itself as fat and fruitful is described as thin, and fields planted with great care yield nothing on the day it matters. Nothing is capricious in the sentence, because the harvest the people planted is the harvest they get.

Fourth, He holds judgment and mercy in the same hand. The prophet says that gleanings will remain, that a few berries survive on the highest branches, and that a day is coming when people turn. God leaves a remnant not because the people deserve one but because He keeps a people for Himself, as Isaiah 10:20-22 and Romans 11:5 insist. He does not rescue them from the disaster, but He rescues them through it, so that what survives has learned where to look.

Fifth, He is the Lord of the sea. The roar of the nations is real, and the text takes it seriously by describing it at length. Then one rebuke ends it. The point is not that God is gentle with hostile powers but that He is not frightened by them, and that the night of terror can be over before morning, as it was outside Jerusalem, Isaiah 37:36.

For worship, this means we are invited to bring our attention, not just our requests. 'Look to your Maker' is an act of praise before it is a plan of action. The chapter trains us to see the Holy One of Israel as the stable center of a world in which every other fortress is on loan, and to pray with the confidence of those who know the roaring waters have a Lord.

crossReferences.note: The historical narrative behind the oracle. Aram and Israel besiege Ahaz, and instead of waiting on the LORD he sends the temple silver to Assyria, which then captures Damascus and kills Rezin. Isaiah 17 is the prophetic reading of what the king's account records as politics.

Isaiah's earlier word to Ahaz. The two enemies are 'smoldering stubs of firewood,' Ephraim will be shattered, and the king is told, 'If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.' Chapter 17 shows what that outcome looks like in full.

Before the boy can say 'Father' or 'Mother,' Damascus and Samaria will be plundered, and then the Assyrian flood will reach Judah. The raging peoples of 8:9 are told to prepare for battle and be shattered, matching the nations of 17:12-14, because 'God is with us.'

Moses' song charges Israel with scorning 'the Rock of his salvation' and forgetting 'the God who gave you birth.' Isaiah 17:10 applies this ancient indictment to the eighth century, which suggests the song was a standard by which later prophets measured the people.

The beaten olive tree and the gleaning after the grape harvest reappear, now describing the whole earth. What happens to Ephraim in chapter 17 becomes a sample of the world's judgment, and the remnant that survives both times is a gift of God, not a byproduct of history.

The prophet's later charge against those who go down to Egypt: they 'do not look to the Holy One of Israel.' The language of looking in 17:7-8 is picked up here for Judah's own temptation, which shows how directly chapter 17 is aimed at the south.

God lays in Zion 'a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken.' It is the positive answer to forgetting the Rock of refuge in 17:10, the stone that holds when Ephraim's refuge of plans and plots does not.

Paul says that Israel drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and 'that rock was Christ.' This is the apostolic key to the title in Isaiah 17:10: the Rock Israel forgot is the one who goes with His people and ultimately comes among them.

A concrete case of the turning promised in 17:7. When Hezekiah invited the north to Passover, many scorned the couriers, but 'some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.' The remnant is made of such persons.

Jesus 'rebuked the wind and the sea,' and the disciples ask who He is. The verb of rebuke and the image of raging waters recall the Old Testament descriptions of God quieting the seas and nations, and Isaiah 17:13, so the question receives its answer.

Paul says God has not rejected His people, for 'at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace,' as in Elijah's day. The gleanings of Isaiah 17:6 are an Old Testament instance of the principle he describes, and a promise that judgment is never total.

study.oneStory:
The chapter sits in the long middle of the Bible's story, where the fall has produced nations at war with each other and with God, and where God is working out His promise to Abraham through a small people in a crowded corner of the world. By the time of Isaiah the story has already run through Babel's scattering, the covenant with Abraham, the exodus, the kingdom of David and the division of the kingdom. The northern tribes are now allied with a pagan neighbour and the southern king is ready to hire a pagan empire, and the question the whole story has been asking is whether this people will look to the LORD or to someone else.

Isaiah 17 answers that question for a particular moment, and the answer has a consistent shape across the Bible. Human strength looks solid and does not last. God does not abandon a faithless people, but He does strip away the false supports until what is left is a remnant that has learned to look to the Maker. That pattern appears in the flood, in Elijah's seven thousand, in the exile and return, and in the church's own history.

The chapter also keeps a thread alive that leads to Jesus. The remnant of Jacob that survives is a fragile chain by which the promise to Abraham reaches the cross. The Rock Israel forgot becomes the cornerstone on which a new people is built, 1 Peter 2:4-6. The nations that rage like the sea are met by the One who rebukes them, and in the end they are not only silenced but gathered. Paul sees this when he reads Isaiah's promise that the Root of Jesse will rise to rule the Gentiles, Romans 15:12.

The end of the story answers the chapter's last cry. In the new creation there is no more roaring sea, because the old order has passed away, Revelation 21:1, and no hostile people to loot and plunder, because the nations walk by the light of the Lamb, Revelation 21:24. The altars made by fingers have been replaced by a city that has no temple because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. What Isaiah 17 asks Judah to do, to look at last to the Maker, is what the redeemed do forever.

quiz.q: Why does this oracle pronounce judgment on Ephraim, Israel's northern kingdom, alongside Damascus?

options.text: Because Israel allied with Aram against Judah instead of trusting the LORD, binding their fates together.
options.note: The Syro-Ephraimite alliance, 2 Kings 16, ties Ephraim's judgment to Damascus's.

options.text: Because Israel and Aram shared a common language and border.
options.note: Geography is not the point; the alliance against Judah and against trust in the LORD is.

options.text: Because Ephraim had also worshiped foreign idols like Aram.
options.note: True and relevant, but the oracle specifically follows their political alliance against Judah.

options.text: Because the two nations happened to be destroyed in the same year by coincidence.
options.note: Scripture presents this as the LORD's deliberate judgment, not coincidence.

quiz.q: What image describes the reduced glory of Jacob after judgment?

options.text: A harvested field and a beaten olive tree left with only a few gleanings.
options.note: Verses 4 to 6 use exactly this image of a nearly stripped harvest.

options.text: A city rebuilt stronger than before.
options.note: The opposite; the chapter describes diminishment, not rebuilding.

options.text: A river that overflows its banks.
options.note: This image belongs to a different oracle, not this one.

options.text: A flock scattered but soon regathered in full.
options.note: Close in spirit to the remnant theme, but the specific image given is the beaten olive tree.

quiz.q: What does the LORD say Israel forgot, according to verse 10?

options.text: The Rock of her refuge, the God of her salvation.
options.note: Verse 10 names exactly this forgetting as the root problem.

options.text: The borders of the Promised Land.
options.note: Not the issue in this text; the failure is spiritual, not geographic.

options.text: The words of the law given at Sinai.
options.note: Related in principle, but the verse specifically names forgetting the Rock of salvation.

options.text: The name of her ally, Aram.
options.note: Israel remembered Aram all too well; the tragedy is forgetting the LORD instead.

quiz.q: How does the chapter end, in verses 12 to 14?

options.text: With the roaring nations suddenly routed, terror in the evening and gone by morning.
options.note: This is the closing picture: a sudden divine reversal of the raging nations.

options.text: With Israel and Aram forming a lasting peace.
options.note: No such resolution appears; the nations are instead scattered.

options.text: With a detailed genealogy of the kings involved.
options.note: Not present in this passage.

options.text: With a slow, drawn-out siege lasting many years.
options.note: The text instead emphasizes suddenness, evening to morning, not a long siege.

quiz.q: How does the forgotten Rock of Isaiah 17 point forward to Christ?

options.text: The New Testament identifies Christ as the spiritual Rock and the tested cornerstone Israel needed.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 10:4 and 1 Peter 2:6, drawing on Isaiah 28:16, make this connection explicit.

options.text: It shows Jesus has no connection to Old Testament rock imagery.
options.note: The opposite is true; Scripture draws this connection directly.

options.text: It suggests rocks were sacred objects in ancient Israelite religion.
options.note: This misses the theological point; the Rock is a title for the LORD, not a sacred object.

options.text: It is only a poetic figure with no further significance.
options.note: It is poetic, but Scripture gives it real theological weight in identifying Christ as that Rock.

questions: Damascus and Ephraim leaned on each other instead of on the LORD, and both fell together. What alliances or securities are you leaning on instead of trusting God?
Even in judgment, the LORD left gleanings on the tree and promised a remnant who would turn to their Maker. Where do you see God's mercy woven through hard circumstances in your own life?
Israel forgot the Rock of her salvation while busily cultivating foreign vines that yielded no harvest. What are you investing your energy in that cannot ultimately give you life?
The nations that roared like mighty waters were suddenly and completely routed. What fears or threats loom large in your life right now that are, in fact, already under God's command?
Christ is revealed as the Rock that Israel forgot. What would it look like this week to consciously remember Him as your refuge rather than trusting in yourself?

translationNotes.note: Burden renders massa, which can mean either a heavy load carried or a solemn oracle; nearly every oracle against a foreign nation in chapters 13 to 23 opens with this same word.
The image compares Israel's remnant to the last few olives left after a harvest beating.
The sentence runs across the verse break, describing a planting that ultimately fails.
